title: Apple’s next big thing may be even riskier than the iPhone Duo
content:
Macworld





This time next week, the Apple world could look very different. We may have received (and doubtless be obsessing over the artwork and tagline of) invitations to an event on October 13, when reputable sources say the company will unveil its next big thing. Or, based on other clues, namely the arrival in Apple retail stores of mysterious boxes to be opened on October 8, the information may have already emerged.
Whether it appears this Thursday or next Tuesday, and whether it’s announced via a big press event or a humble press release, Apple’s next big thing will almost certainly be its first bona fide smart-home product: a hub, made up of a vaguely HomePod-like speaker topped by a vaguely iPad-like screen. We in the media have taken to calling it the HomePad, but if the recent launches of the MacBook Neo and iPhone Duo are anything to go by, Apple will probably call it something short and cute and random, ending with an O. The HomePod Echo, perhaps. Or perhaps not.
The real issue with the HomePad is not its name, but its niche. Potential customers will ask every marketing manager’s most feared question: What is it for? If Apple hasn’t come up with an answer in the multiple years the product has been in development, it’s unlikely something will spring to mind in the next eight days. But one way or another an answer will be needed.
As I hinted with my silly Echo joke, this isn’t an unprecedented concept or a new market. Amazon’s closest rival is probably the Echo Show 8 (the Show 5 is closer in screen size, but has a different design), while Google has the Nest Hub, and both sit in the space Apple will be looking to dominate. The presence of these incumbents might seem like a good omen for the company, which loves to wait until a market is established before taking a swing with the definitive product. But as with the foldable iPhone Duo, there are two problems: First, while tech fans in general are intimately familiar with the concept, Apple’s own fans are not. And second, Apple’s version is likely to be more expensive.
The original HomePod may be an illustrative comparison here. Apple was expected to go after the smart speaker market, but ended up leaning far more on the second word than the first. The HomePod is sort of smart, but it’s really just a nice, decent-quality speaker you can command (some of the time…) using your voice. And so Apple didn’t end up displacing products like the Echo and the Nest because the HomePod couldn’t do what they do and didn’t really try, while overachieving in other areas and costing more. And Apple customers, unless they were bold enough to become platform-agnostic, remained outside that bubble.
Siri is a lot smarter now than it was then (not that you’d know it from the performance of legacy HomePod models, unfortunately), so the chances are that Apple will try to do the smart-home concept properly this time. The HomePad will run Siri AI, and thus be able to field questions, surface information from your messages and email inbox, and use natural language. It will have excellent capabilities. But again, the question is what we will use these capabilities for. Where will it sit? What functions will it perform? Speaking personally, I’m not sure how it would fit in my life. So the product’s introduction will need to do a great deal of imaginative heavy lifting.
Let’s say the HomePad sits in the kitchen. Useful for recipes, perhaps, although it’s important to remember that it will only have a 6-inch screen and thus won’t match an iPad for legibility. Or it might sit in the living room and act as the hub for smart-home controls. But what proportion of Apple fans actually use HomeKit smart lights, smart door locks, and a smart thermostat so much that they need a dedicated device? A relatively small one, I’d guess, and those that do will be accustomed to controlling them via automations or manual control on an iPhone. Or even voice controls via a HomePod.
At least with the iPhone Duo, Apple had some user experience to lean on. It is, after all, still a phone, albeit one that’s a little smaller than we’re used to, with the ability to offer a bigger screen than we’re used to. But customers get what it’s offering. It’s a phone, only conceptually better. (And pragmatically, in some ways, rather worse.) You don’t need to make such an imaginative leap of faith.
But the HomePad doesn’t really have a precedent in Apple’s walled garden. It’s a HomePod with a screen. But having a screen (and offering voice control which actually works) massively expands its capabilities in one area, while cutting the speaker down to a tiny hemisphere, as is predicted, slashes them in another. What we end up with isn’t remotely like a HomePod in form or function. It’s something new. And new is scary.
So Apple’s crack marketing team has another challenge on their hands. If you thought the iPhone Duo was an exciting, radical, risky product, wait for the HomePad.
Or whatever they end up calling it. Something short and cute and random. Ending with an O.

title: iPhone 18 Pro & Max Guide: Everything you need to know about the new iPhones
content:
Macworld





The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are now on sale. They retain the 6.3-inch and 6.9-inch screen sizes and aluminum unibody design introduced with the previous generation, but Apple has made substantial changes to the cameras, processor, cooling, battery life and connectivity.
The biggest camera upgrade is a new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture, which can automatically move between ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8 and ƒ/4 depending on lighting and depth of field. The widest aperture lets in more light for low-light photography, while new Pro controls let users manually adjust aperture, shutter speed and white balance, and view a histogram to assess exposure.
Inside is the A20 Pro, Apple’s first iPhone chip made using a 2nm process. It has a new six-core CPU, seven-core GPU, Dual 16-core Neural Engine and 50% more memory bandwidth than the A19 Pro. A larger vapor chamber and new M-series-inspired chip packaging also improve heat dissipation, with Apple claiming up to 40% better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro.
Other major changes include up to 36 hours of Apple-rated video playback on the Pro and 45 hours on the Pro Max on eSIM-only models, faster wired charging, and a redesigned Dynamic Island capable of showing three Live Activities simultaneously. The iPhone 18 Pro uses Apple’s new C2 cellular modem worldwide. The Pro Max also uses C2 outside the U.S., but teardown analysis has confirmed that the U.S. iPhone 18 Pro Max retains Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X80 modem – more on that below.
Since launch, some owners have also reported problems including unexpected restarts, touchscreen freezes and speaker crackling or popping. Apple addressed several early issues in iOS 27.0.1, although the cause of the reported speaker problem remains unclear.
iPhone 18 Pro/Max vs iPhone 17 Pro/Max: Top 10 changes at a glance

				
					

				
			iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro
Foundry




The five biggest changes are the variable-aperture camera, A20 Pro, improved cooling, longer battery life and redesigned Dynamic Island/connectivity system. Here is an overview of what’s new compared to the previous generation.

Apple has added a 2TB option to the smaller Pro for the first time, while retaining 256GB as the entry-level capacity.


When is the iPhone 18 Pro coming out? Availability and how to buy
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max were announced on Wednesday, September 9, 2026 and started shipping on Friday, September 18, 2026 in more than 65 countries and regions and in another 20 countries from Friday September 25.
You can buy the phones directly from Apple online or at Apple Stores, as well as through mobile networks and authorized Apple retailers. Apple sells unlocked iPhones directly through its website and stores. We have tips on when is the Best time to buy an iPhone if you want to get the best deal or avoid buying just before a new iPhone launches.

iPhone 18 Pro problems: What owners are reporting
Owners of the new iPhone 18 Pro models have already reported a number of issues since the phones went on sale.
It isn’t clear how widespread these problems are, but Apple released iOS 27.0.1 on September 28 with fixes for several issues affecting the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
If you’re experiencing any of the problems addressed by the update, install iOS 27.0.1 via Settings > General > Software Update. 
Cellular problems on some AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max phones
Apple has confirmed that a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on AT&T can lose cellular service, preventing calls, texts and data access, potentially including 911 calls. Complaints began shortly after launch, with some users reporting their phones dropping into SOS mode despite showing a strong 5G signal. 
Apple says owners should install iOS 27.0.1 as well as a new carrier settings update. Together, the updates are intended to prevent the problem from occurring. The carrier update should install automatically within 14 days, or users can check manually by going to Settings > General > About. 
However, the updates cannot repair phones that have already lost service because of the issue. Apple says affected devices cannot be reactivated through software and will need to be replaced, with customers advised to contact Apple or AT&T for assistance.
The exact cause remains unknown. One key difference is that the U.S. iPhone 18 Pro Max uses Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X80 modem, while the iPhone 18 Pro uses Apple’s C2 modem, but there is no evidence that Qualcomm hardware itself is to blame. The X80 was also used without this problem in earlier iPhones, and the issue appears more likely to involve the way the phone’s software and hardware interact with AT&T’s network.
Unexpected restarts after Face ID failed to authenticate
Some ownersApple says iOS 27.0.1 addresses the touchscreen problem reported that their phones would freeze and restart after a failed Face ID attempt, particularly when trying to unlock protected apps.
According to Apple’s release notes for iOS 27.0.1, the update fixes an issue that could cause an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max to unexpectedly restart after Face ID failed to authenticate.
Camera color artifact bug
iOS 27.0.1 also fixes a camera bug that could cause a color artifact to appear in photos taken at 2x under certain lighting conditions at f/1.48 on a small number of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max devices.
Touchscreen problem
Some owners reported a problem with the iPhone 18 Pro’s screen where opening Notification Center and Control Center simultaneously could cause the display to become unresponsive.
Apple says iOS 27.0.1 fixes the touchscreen problem.
Speaker crackling and popping
Some iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max owners are reporting intermittent crackling, popping, or clicking sounds from the phone’s speakers, particularly the earpiece during calls. Reports on Apple’s support forums describe the problem occurring randomly rather than on every call, with some users saying that restarting the iPhone temporarily clears it. Others have encountered similar noises during video calls or while using certain apps.
It isn’t yet clear whether the problem is caused by the iPhone 18 Pro hardware or by iOS 27. There are reports of replacement phones exhibiting the same behavior, while at least one user has reported similar call-quality problems on an older iPhone after updating to iOS 27, raising the possibility that software is involved.
iOS 27.0.1 does not appear to address the issue, and Apple has not publicly confirmed a cause or fix at this stage.


						

							


iPhone 18 Pro/Max design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			
This is the Burgundy variant (we think Deep Cherry was a much nicer name).

Foundry




The iPhone 18 Pro retains the aluminum unibody introduced with the iPhone 17 Pro, as well as the Ceramic Shield on the rear and Ceramic Shield 2 over the display. The camera system remains arranged on the large raised plateau across the upper part of the rear casing.
Screen sizes are unchanged at 6.3 inches for the iPhone 18 Pro and 6.9 inches for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, both using Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz.
Apple offers four finishes this year:
Burgundy 
Glacier
Silver
Black
That means Cosmic Orange and Deep Blue disappear, while black returns to the Pro line despite pre-launch reports suggesting it would not. Read more about the color choices here: Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro colors.
The pre-event leaks suggested the basic chassis dimensions would remain very close to the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, with the camera plateau rather than the body itself becoming thicker. We can confirm from our own research that the newer camera bump is approximately 0.5mm taller. This means that cases designed for the iPhone 17 Pro may not fit the iPhone 18 Pro. Before buying a case, check compatibility and  read our Best iPhone 18 Pro cases buying guide.
The new iPhones share the same screen sizes and overall form as their predecessors, but both models are slightly heavier this time. 
iPhone 18 Pro dimensions: 150 x 71.9 x 8.75mm / 5.91 x 2.83 x 0.34 in
iPhone 18 Pro weight: 7.44 ounces / 211 grams (17 Pro was 7.27 ounces / 206 grams with eSIM)
iPhone 18 Pro Max dimensions: 163.4 x 78 x 8.75mm / 6.43 x 3.07 x 0.34 in
iPhone 18 Pro Max weight: 8.78 ounces / 249 grams (17 Pro Max was 8.22 ounces / 233 grams with eSIM)
Changes to the Dynamic Island
Apple has redesigned the Dynamic Island. Apple says new display technology creates additional usable space and allows the Dynamic Island to display up to three Live Activities at once, for example navigation, music and a sports score.
Apple has not announced fully under-display Face ID. Pre-launch reports suggested that one or more infrared Face ID components could move beneath the OLED panel, allowing the notch to shrink, but Apple hasn’t confirmed the underlying sensor arrangement.


						

							


iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max cameras: Are the cameras the same?

				
					

				
			
The iPhone 18 Pro cameras.

Apple




Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have the same three-camera rear system. The main change is not resolution—all three remain 48MP—but the new variable-aperture Main camera and new computational imaging pipeline.
The three most notable camera upgrades are:
Variable aperture on the 48MP Main camera.
A new Main camera sensor and imaging pipeline, improving low-light performance and detail.
More extensive manual Pro controls, including aperture, shutter speed, white balance and histogram.


						

							




Rear cameras

Fusion Main48MP sensor; 12MP at 2x optical-quality zoom24mm / 48mm, 1x / 2xƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, ƒ/4 variable2.44μm quad-pixel / 1.22μm individual

The 2x and 8x optical-quality options use crops from the Main and Telephoto sensors respectively, producing 12MP images rather than 48MP captures.
The Main camera’s six-blade mechanical aperture can automatically open to ƒ/1.48 in low light or close as far as ƒ/4 for increased depth of field. Photographers can also select aperture manually.
An iFixIt teardown revealed that the mechanical aperture uses six overlapping, extremely thin blades controlled inside the camera assembly. The mechanism itself is unlikely to be repairable individually if it fails, meaning the complete camera module will probably need to be replaced.
Both Pro models also offer up to 8x optical-quality zoom from the Telephoto camera. Contrary to some earlier rumors, the variable-aperture camera is not exclusive to the Pro Max.


Photography and editing improvements
Computational photography: Apple has introduced a new imaging pipeline, smart focus tracking, improved Clean Up, Spatial Reframing, an Extend tool and Photographic Styles 3, which adds texture and grain adjustments. These controls require photos captured on iPhone 18 Pro/Max or the Duo’s Main, Ultra Wide or Center Stage cameras. Older supported iPhones can edit those eligible images—it isn’t simply a restriction on the editing device. See: Apple’s next-gen photo controls only work on images ‘captured’ on a new iPhone.
Apple Reference Image (U.S. and U.K.): Will use signed data from the iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera sensor to create an unalterable reference image through Private Cloud Compute. Viewed alongside the edited photo in Photos, it helps users assess what has changed, providing a useful authenticity check for photographers, journalists and anyone sharing images. It’s off by default, to enable it go to: Settings > Camera > Reference Image > Add Reference Mode.
Front camera
Apple has retained the 18MP Center Stage front camera, rather than moving to the rumored 24MP sensor. It supports automatic reframing, Center Stage, ultra-stabilized video and Dual Capture.
The front camera remains visibly associated with the Dynamic Island. Apple has not announced an under-display selfie camera on the iPhone 18 Pro.
iPhone 18 Pro video changes
Frame rates: Cinematic effects can now be applied after shooting to ordinary videos captured at up to 60fps. The phones continue to offer 4K 120fps Dolby Vision for high-frame-rate shooting.
Time-lapse: Time-lapse receives a significant upgrade to 4K with Dolby Vision HDR.


						

							


A20 Pro processor: How fast is it?

				
					

				
			
Apple has redesigned the iPhone chip. 

Apple




Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max use Apple’s new A20 Pro processor.
It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, down from the 3nm-class process used for A19 Pro, giving Apple more scope to improve efficiency and transistor density.
The chip includes:
6-core CPU
7-core GPU
Neural Accelerators integrated into the CPU/GPU architecture
Dual 16-core Neural Engine, 32 cores in total
50% more memory bandwidth than A19 Pro
Apple says the GPU is up to 40% faster than A19 Pro, while the Neural Engine offers roughly double the AI processing capability.
One particularly important change is the packaging. Inspired by Apple’s M-series Mac chips, A20 Pro places the processor die side-by-side with memory rather than stacking memory directly in the chip’s thermal path. This improves heat transfer and allows the processor to couple more directly to the vapor chamber.
That vapor chamber itself has three times the surface area of the iPhone 17 Pro’s system. Apple claims the combination delivers up to 40% better sustained performance, which should be most noticeable during gaming, video work and intensive on-device AI rather than ordinary web browsing and messaging.
During our review, the iPhone 18 Pro showed noticeably less heat buildup than the iPhone 17 Pro when playing demanding games, recording extended video and performing other prolonged intensive tasks. It still became warm. This was our reviewer’s observation during use, rather than a measured temperature reduction or a quantified test of Apple’s sustained-performance claim.


						

							


RAM: How much memory does the iPhone 18 Pro/Max have?
Apple does not officially publish RAM capacities for iPhones. However, iFixIt lists 12GB of LPDDR5X memory for both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, matching the reported 12GB in the previous Pro generation.
The main memory upgrade is bandwidth: Apple says the A20 Pro offers 50% more memory bandwidth than A19 Pro. This increases the amount of data its CPU, GPU and Neural Engine can transfer to and from memory each second.
Higher memory bandwidth can help accelerate demanding tasks, including on-device AI. Combined with the redesigned chip packaging and improved cooling, it should help sustain performance during intensive workloads. However, this does not necessarily mean that more Apple Intelligence or Siri AI tasks run locally rather than in the cloud.


						

							


iPhone 18 Pro/Max connectivity options 
C2 modem
The iPhone 18 Pro introduces Apple’s C2 cellular modem, replacing the Qualcomm modem used in the previous Pro generation. 
Apple says C2 delivers faster uploads while consuming 15% less energy than C1X, alongside AI-powered improvements to connection quality and reliability and support for mmWave in the U.S.
The exception is the U.S. iPhone 18 Pro Max. iFixIt’s teardowns have confirmed that this version retains Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X80 modem, while Pro Max models sold elsewhere use Apple’s C2. Apple has not explained the regional difference.
Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
Like the predecessors, the 2026 iPhones use Apple’s N1 wireless networking chip, supporting:
Wi-Fi 7
Bluetooth 6
Thread
Satellite
Emergency SOS via satellite, Messages via satellite, Roadside Assistance via satellite and Find My satellite functionality continue. Apple made no announcements about full satellite internet or ordinary 5G data delivered by satellite, despite pre-launch rumors suggesting such a capability could appear.


						

							


iPhone 18 Pro/Max Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s changed?
Battery life is one of the most significant improvements.
Apple says eSIM-only models gain additional battery capacity because the space previously occupied by the physical SIM tray can be used for battery cells. Physical-SIM variants provide around two hours less video playback than equivalent eSIM-only models.
Battery-life improvements come from larger batteries and greater power efficiency, including the new 2nm A20 Pro processor.


						

							




iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max battery capacity and life
The table below compares battery capacity and Apple’s video-playback ratings for the physical-SIM and eSIM-only versions of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.


ModelSIM versionBattery capacityEnergyVideo playbackEquivalent iPhone 17 model: video playbackImprovement

iPhone 18 ProeSIM-only4,288mAh16.76WhUp to 36 hours17 Pro: up to 33 hours+3 hours

iPhone 18 Pro MaxeSIM-only5,567mAh21.75WhUp to 45 hours17 Pro Max: up to 39 hours+6 hours

 



We discuss the battery life for different iPhones in more depth separately. 


Wired charging
Wired charging is faster. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max can reach 50% charge in around 15 minutes when using a USB-C cable and a 60W-capable or higher power adapter that supports Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS). The adapter is sold separately. This compares with around 20 minutes for the iPhone 17 Pro generation. Apple also says five minutes of wired charging can provide around seven hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro Max.
Our charging tests also showed an improvement: the iPhone 18 Pro reached 80 percent charge about 10 minutes sooner than the iPhone 17 Pro, and a full charge almost 20 minutes sooner. These results apply to the smaller Pro model.
MagSafe and wireless charging
Apple says both models can reach 50% charge in around 30 minutes using a MagSafe Charger paired with a 35W or higher power adapter, both sold separately. MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging support up to 25W. Wireless charging speeds are broadly unchanged from the iPhone 17 Pro generation.


						

							


iPhone 18 Pro software: iOS 27 and Siri AI 
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max support Siri AI in iOS 27, but the upgraded assistant isn’t enabled automatically. 
To request access, open Settings > Siri, enable Siri if necessary, then tap Try Siri AI (Beta). 
Then follow the setup instructions to join Apple’s waiting list. 
Access may arrive within minutes, hours or days, with a notification when it’s ready. 
Your device and Siri languages must both be English, and availability depends on your Apple Account region. You may also need up to 14GB of free storage. See how to get Siri AI for setup instructions and details of regional restrictions.


						

							




iPhone 18 Pro price: How much does it cost?
Apple has increased prices by $100 in the U.S. and £100 in the U.K. 
The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. Both begin with 256GB of storage.


ModeliPhone 18 starting priceiPhone 17 starting priceChange
iPhone Pro$1,199/£1,199$1,099/£1,099+$100/£100
iPhone Pro Max$1,299/£1,299$1,199/£1,199+$100/£100

 



Apple offers both models with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB. That means the entry-level storage remains 256GB rather than increasing again. The notable change is that 2TB is now available on both models; previously the iPhone 17 Pro topped out at 1TB while the Pro Max could be configured with 2TB.
The $100 increase is considerably smaller than some analyst predictions before launch. Those forecasts had pointed to sharply higher DRAM and NAND costs caused by the global memory shortage, with estimates that the cost of 12GB of DRAM alone could rise dramatically this year. That makes component and memory pricing a credible contributor to Apple’s increase, although Apple itself hasn’t attributed the higher price to any one component.


Should you buy the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max? Which model should you choose?

				
					

				
			
Which one do you want?

Apple




The iPhone 18 Pro is the better-value Pro model for most buyers, offering the same cameras and A20 Pro processor as the Pro Max in a more manageable 6.3-inch design. Choose the Pro Max if its 6.9-inch display and longer battery life justify the extra $100/£100 and additional weight. Apple rates it for up to 45 hours of video playback on eSIM-only models, or 43 hours on physical-SIM versions.
However, you may not need a Pro iPhone at all. Our best iPhone guide recommends the standard iPhone 17 for most people: its ProMotion display, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage cover everyday needs for considerably less. Paying extra for the 18 Pro makes most sense if you want its dedicated Telephoto camera, variable aperture or additional performance for demanding games and creative work.
iPhone 17 Pro owners don’t need to rush to upgrade. Consider whether the variable-aperture Main camera, A20 Pro, improved cooling, faster charging and longer battery life will make enough difference to justify the expense. If your current phone comfortably handles everything you do, keeping it is a sensible choice.
For iPhone 14 Pro owners and earlier, the accumulated improvements make a stronger case. You gain USB-C, Apple Intelligence compatibility, higher-resolution Ultra Wide and Telephoto cameras, an improved front camera, larger displays and slimmer bezels. These changes span several generations: USB-C and the Action button arrived before Camera Control and the larger Pro displays, while the 18MP Center Stage front camera was already available on the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple Intelligence also supports the iPhone 15 Pro and later compatible models. This year’s variable aperture, A20 Pro and further battery improvements build on those earlier upgrades. Read why the iPhone 18 Pro rewards those who waited.
The iPhone Duo is worth considering if screen space and multitasking matter more than camera versatility. Its folding display and Split View offer something the Pro models cannot, but its $1,999/£1,999 starting price is $800/£800 above the smaller Pro. Despite that premium, it lacks a dedicated Telephoto camera and variable aperture. Choose the Duo for its folding design; choose a Pro for photography and better value. Our iPhone buying guide compares the specifications.
Both Pro models are now on sale, making this a good point in their release cycle to buy. If saving money matters more than upgrading immediately, Black Friday may bring better trade-in or carrier offers, although large outright discounts are unlikely so soon after launch. A substantially discounted iPhone 17 Pro is another option. See the best time to buy an iPhone.


						

							


Did Apple launch the iPhone 18?
There was no new iPhone 18 at the event. We expect the iPhone 18 to launch alongside the iPhone 18e and iPhone Air 2 in spring 2027. Read more about the iPhone 18 here: iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e: Release date, rumored specs and more.

title: Apple's New CEO John Ternus is Making Product Design a 'Major Priority'
content:
Since becoming Apple's CEO last month, John Ternus has made product design a "major priority," according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. 


"Ternus already had some involvement with the design studio as Apple's head of hardware engineering, given the close coordination required between the two functions," he said, in his Power On newsletter today. "Since becoming CEO, however, he has immersed himself in the industrial design and human interface teams."

Ternus goes "hands-on" in Apple's design studio "several times a week, sometimes visiting multiple times in a single day," whereas Apple's former CEO Tim Cook typically visited the studio for "about an hour once a month, at most," according to Gurman.

Unlike Cook, who is better known as a supply chain expert, Ternus comes from an engineering background. As such, Gurman said that Ternus is largely leaving Apple's finances to financial chief Kevan Parekh and its supply chain to operations chief Sabih Khan, giving him more time to focus on engineering and design.

title: Apple confirms iPhone cellular issue, admits affected units can’t be fixed
content:
Macworld





Following numerous complaints from iPhone 18 Pro Max owners, it’s now been officially acknowledged that some units have a problem placing calls, sending texts, and accessing data. Initially by the carrier AT&T, which sent out a message to customers warning about the issue and strongly advising them to update iOS “immediately”. And now by Apple itself.
As seen by MacRumors, the carrier sent out the following text on Thursday:
“Hi, it’s AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately — Settings > General > Software Update. Please contact AT&T or Apple if you have questions.”
While this formal admission will be some comfort to affected parties–since the first step on the road to a fix is admitting that one is needed–the proposed solution may not be viewed kindly. Apple’s release notes for the iOS 27.0.1 software update do not mention fixing this issue. And many users who’ve encountered the bug explicitly report that updating to 27.0.1 doesn’t fix it.
The problem was first reported in mid-September. “New [iPhone 18 Pro Max] can’t make or receive phone calls or FaceTime,” complained the author of one Apple Support discussion thread. “Text messages are extremely slow to come through… It does all of this even when the phone is showing four bars of 5G… then the phone randomly drops service and goes into SOS.”
A Redditor, meanwhile, wrote: “I got my iPhone 18 on Friday. I have coverage through AT&T. I have been noticing that I have been getting SOS on my phone. Wi-Fi works for the internet but I can’t make calls. Even if it doesn’t say SOS, trying to make a phone call is impossible now.”
There are thousands of replies to these and similar discussions, many of whom confirm they’ve had the same experience. And they are pessimistic about AT&T’s solution. One commenter on the Apple Support thread replies, “I just received a text from them that the latest [iOS 27.0.1] update would fix the problem – I had already updated to this so I know it isn’t the resolution. This just reaffirms that they have no idea what the problem is or how to fix it.”
And while a separate Reddit thread entitled “iPhone 18 Pro Max Cellular Issues: Did iOS 27.0.1 resolve them?” includes a couple of replies who cautiously think it may have helped, the overwhelming majority of people are unconvinced the issue is fixed:
“No, it did not fix that issue. Can confirm personally.”
“No… The bugfix update did nothing.”
“I feel like the 27.0.1 update made it worse.”
“I did the update but still have the problem.”
“I’m still having the issue even after the update, so it’s definitely AT&T.”
“I updated and it didn’t fix it and had to get the phone replaced for SECOND time.”
After we initially posted this article, AT&T contacted Macworld and asked us to publish a statement:
“Apple has released a software update to address an issue that may affect calls, data, texts, and 911 calls on a small number of Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max phones. AT&T customers with an iPhone 18 Pro Max should update their phones now to the latest available software. Our top priority is ensuring customers can stay connected when they need it most, and we are working with Apple to make it right.”
Based on the unsatisfied responses of affected parties, however, this didn’t seem convincing. At this point, it wasn’t even clear if it was a hardware or software problem, let alone whether it was possible to fix it through an iOS update. Resolution looked to be a long way off.
Apple gets involved
On October 3, Apple got in touch to offer a company statement and a fix. But it’s not entirely good news.
“We have identified an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls,” said an Apple spokesperson. “We released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and strongly encourage all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update now, and are also issuing a carrier settings update today. These updates together are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring.”
The company believes that the iPhone 18 Pro Max problem can be avoided (that’s to say, avoided in the future, not fixed if it’s already happened) if users install iOS 27.0.1 and the latest carrier settings update. You need both to be protected, apparently. AT&T-based iPhone 18 Pro Max owners should find that the carrier settings update downloads automatically within the next 14 days, but they can manually trigger this process by opening Settings and going to General > About.
But this is a prophylactic measure, not a cure. If an iPhone has already been affected and is therefore without service, Apple admits that it cannot be reactivated via software and will require a hardware replacement. In such cases, the owner should contact Apple Support or AT&T, or visit an Apple Store or AT&T location.

title: Apple tightens macOS Full Disk Access controls as AI agents proliferate
content:
Macworld





If you’ve been using third-party apps on your Mac, you are probably familiar with a permission dialog box called “Full Disk Access.” It’s sort of a big catch-all permission that lets an application read or write almost any data to your Mac’s drive.
It was originally conceived as a way for apps to be able to fully back up and restore your hard drive, but developers have since used it as a shortcut for auto-updating apps, managment apps, among others. On my Mac, the Adobe Creative Cloud updater wants this permission, as does the Logitech software for managing my keyboard and mouse, and Microsoft OneDrive.
AI agents on the Mac also typically ask for this permission, and it allows them to access information that you may not iwant them to have. If you know where the data is stored, you can access full messages, contacts, photos, emails, browsing history, and much more with just this one setting.
In a note on its Developer Site, Apple says it’s about to crack down on this Full Disk Access abuse by introducing additional controls:
We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users’ private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.
Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action. Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.
Apple has not yet said what form these controls will take, but it’s likely that it’ll start with sterner wording for this setting, making it clear that any app that requests this access can essentialy see everything on your drive, including every cache and buffer storing info from online services.
We’re starting to hear plenty of horror stories about AI agents having knowledge they’re not supposed to have or wreaking havoc by deleting or modifying important files, and they almost always stem from this simple and over-permissive setting granting access to read and write almost every file on your Mac.
Apple has not given a time frame for this Full Disk Access abuse crackdown, but given how many applications (not just AI agents) use it when they don’t really need to access your entire Mac disk, it can’t come soon enough.

title: How to send photos as email attachments on the iPhone
content:
Macworld





Since iOS 14, there is no longer an option to send photos as attachments. Apple changed the creation of new emails on iOS so that as soon as any additional formatting is used, the message is no longer sent as plain text but as an HTML email. As a result, inserted images are automatically displayed within the email and are not sent as separate attachments.
Apple doesn’t seem like it will change this soon. Here are some tips for sending emails with images from the iPhone.
How to send iPhone photos as attachments
Use a different email app. To avoid embedded photos in emails, the most reliable method is to use a third-party email app such as Microsoft Outlook app on your iPhone and use it only to send photos.
Outlook for iOS is available for free from the App Store. You can use the app as a standard email client, even if you don’t have a Microsoft subscription. When sending emails, remember to send the photos via Outlook rather than the Mail app. Since iOS 18, you can set a third-party email app as the default.
Zip the photos. Another method is to send your iPhone photos as an archived ZIP file. This can be done using a shortcut called ‘Zip and Share Photos’, which we’ve made available for download through this link. Once you’ve installed the shortcut in the Shortcuts app, open your Photos library and tap the Share button on any image. In the Share menu, select the Zip and Share Photos option and then select the images you want. After tapping Add, you can select your preferred email client.
The iPhone will then create a Zip file containing the original images and attach it to the email. By default, the file is named after the device name and the current date. If desired, you can customize the automatically generated filename by adding your own variables or text blocks in the second step of the shortcut.
Print to PDF. Another method does not require any third-party apps, but it has one drawback: the selected photos are combined into a single file. To do this, use the iPhone’s built-in print function. Open the Photos app, select one or more images and tap the share arrow in the bottom-left corner.
In the Share menu, rather than selecting an app such as Mail or Messages directly, select the printer icon. The selected photos will then be displayed in a print preview, which initially suggests sending them to an available printer. Then tap the Share arrow again and send the PDF file via your preferred email service. Multiple photos will automatically be distributed across individual PDF pages and can be saved by the recipient as attachments.
Send via iCloud link. To do this, select the photos you want, tap the share icon and choose Create Shared Album Link from the menu. This requires the photos to be synchronized via iCloud. This option is not available if iCloud Photo Library is not enabled. When the recipient opens the link in a browser, they can then download all the shared images in one go.

In the 15 years since it first appeared on the iPhone, Apple’s Find My technology has transformed from a simple GPS-based phone finder to a versatile ecosystem of devices not just from Apple but many specialized accessory makers in all exciting shapes, sizes, and forms. 
Apple’s Find My app offers a unified, secure way to locate all your Apple devices (iPhone, Watch, AirPods, and Mac) and items (AirTags plus third-party trackers such as these reviewed here) via an anonymous network of millions of Apple devices that ping encrypted Bluetooth to report their location back to iCloud, even when offline. Find My helps you to locate misplaced items in seconds, alerts you if you leave them behind, and works through your Apple device.

title: Apple Says iPhone 18 Pro Max Users With AT&T Cellular Issue Need to Have Device Replaced
content:
Apple today confirmed that a "small number" of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network have experienced an issue that causes the device to lose cellular service, thereby preventing phone calls, text messages, and data from working. Thousands of users complained about the issue across the Apple Support Community and other platforms.


Apple said it released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and an AT&T carrier settings update earlier today to help prevent more iPhone 18 Pro Max users from being impacted by this issue going forward. In a statement shared with MacRumors, Apple strongly encouraged all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update to iOS 27.0.1 now. To install the update, open the Settings app on your iPhone and tap on General → Software Update.

The carrier settings update for the iPhone 18 Pro Max will automatically download for AT&T users over the next 14 days, according to Apple. To manually trigger the update, users can open the Settings app and tap on General → About.

We have identified an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls. We released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and strongly encourage all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update now, and are also issuing a carrier settings update today. These updates together are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring.
Notably, Apple said that iPhone 18 Pro Max devices that have been affected by this cellular issue on the AT&T network cannot have service reactivated with a software update. Instead, Apple said the device must be replaced entirely, and it advises affected customers to contact Apple Support or AT&T, or visit an Apple Store or AT&T location.

Apple said it has only observed this issue with iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network. No other iPhone models or carriers are known to be impacted.

Apple did not disclose the underlying cause of the issue. U.S. models of the iPhone 18 Pro Max rely on Qualcomm's Snapdragon X80 modem for cellular connectivity, while variants of the device sold in all other countries are equipped with Apple's custom C2 modem. It is unclear if this modem difference is a factor in this AT&T issue.

Apple Service Program dedicated to this issue. In the meantime, it sounds like Apple Stores will replace affected iPhone 18 Pro Max devices for free, so book an appointment with the Genius Bar if necessary.

title: Apple Announces 'Full Disk Access' Changes on macOS Due to AI Agents
content:
In a post on its developer news website today, Apple announced that it will be introducing "additional controls" for the "Full Disk Access" setting on macOS due to new risks posed by AI agents. This announcement comes amid the rise of always-on AI agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots, which have prompted privacy concerns.


"Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users' full knowledge and understanding," said Apple.

"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," it added.

We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users' private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users' full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.

Apple did not say when the new "Full Disk Access" controls will be implemented.

What it’s about: A limited-series adaptation of the Edith Wharton novel The Custom of the Country. The novel, published in the early 20th century, is about a midwestern girl who climbs the ladder of New York high society.
Important names: The big one is Sofia Coppola, who is developing the series for Apple. No word yet on whether she will direct it.
When you can watch: No release date yet.
El Gato Negro
What it’s about: Based on Richard Dominguez’s comic book about an aging luchador who teams up with his grandson to use the El Gato Negro persona to fight crime in South Texas.
Important names: Robert Rodriguez will direct and produce, while Diego Boneta will star and also produce.
When you can watch: No release date yet.
Brie Larson CIA biography series
What it’s about: A report in Variety says that Apple has made a direct-to-series order for a new drama based on the real-life experiences of CIA undercover operative Amaryllis Fox. Fox has a hot novel named Life Undercover: Coming of Age in the CIA that released in October 2019. 
Important names: Brie Larson will star and executive produce the series.
When you can watch: No release date yet.
You Think It, I’ll Say It
What it’s about:  According to Variety, Apple has ordered a 10-episode, half-hour run of a new comedy variety show. The show is inspired by Curtis Sittenfeld’s collection of short stories You Think It, I’ll Say It.
Important names: SNL alum Kristen Wiig was set to star, but pulled out citing scheduling conflicts with Wonder Woman 1984. The show is created and produced by Colleen McGuinness (30 Rock, About a Boy).
When you can watch: This project does not yet have a title or release date.

title: Apple plans fix as Microsoft's Exchange shutdown disrupts Mac email
content:
Apple is working on a fix for Exchange access in its Mac apps as Microsoft retires the connection they rely on.


Apple plans Mac Mail fix as Microsoft phases out EWS
The disruption concerns work or school accounts hosted through Microsoft's Exchange Online service. This can disrupt Mail, Calendar, Contacts, Notes, and Reminders, while Apple prepares an update and administrators retain temporary options.
A reader from Old Dominion University forwarded an IT notice reporting problems accessing university email through Apple's built-in Mail app. The notice recommends Mac users switch to Outlook and says iPhone and iPad apps are unaffected.

title: Judge gives Google legal permission to steal content for AI summaries
content:
A US judge has said he's sympathetic to publishers who are losing money because of Google's AI summaries stealing content, but he's not going to do anything to stop it.


Google has had an antitrust case dismissed
Google recently escaped having its search and advertising business split over antitrust accusations from the Department of Justice. But it has been facing multiple other antitrust cases and now there's one fewer.
According to Reuters, Google's parent company Alphabet had convinced a US federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit. It had been brought by Penske Media Corp, best known for publishing Rolling Stone magazine, and Chegg.

title: AT&T on iPhone 18 Pro Max Issues: 'We Are Working With Apple'
content:
In a statement shared with MacRumors today, AT&T said it is "working with Apple" to resolve iPhone 18 Pro Max cellular issues.


"Apple has released a software update to address an issue that may affect calls, data, texts, and 911 calls on a small number of Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max phones," an AT&T spokesperson said. "AT&T customers with an iPhone 18 Pro Max should update their phones now to the latest available software. Our top priority is ensuring customers can stay connected when they need it most, and we are working with Apple to make it right."

reported last week, affected iPhone 18 Pro Max users are unable to connect to the AT&T network for phone calls, text messages, or data either persistently or intermittently, and their devices typically enter SOS mode as a result. The underlying cause has not been confirmed, and Apple has yet to publicly comment on the matter.

Apple Support Community, Reddit, MacRumors Forums, and other online platforms.

equipped with a Qualcomm cellular modem. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo are equipped with Apple's C2 modem worldwide, as is the iPhone 18 Pro Max in all other countries. However, it is unclear if this is a contributing factor.

AT&T said iPhone 18 Pro Max users who have experienced or continue to experience issues can return to an Apple or AT&T store for additional support.

advising them to update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately, even though that update does not appear to resolve the issues, according to comments shared by affected users.

shared on Reddit today, AT&T clarified that its guidance about updating to iOS 27.0.1 is meant to help mitigate future impacts, but it is unclear if or how the update actually helps. Apple's release notes for iOS 27.0.1 only mentioned fixes for other bugs, including a Face ID issue affecting iPhone 18 Pro models.

The alleged email added that customers can visit an Apple or AT&T store for a replacement device, but some customers said their request for a replacement under warranty was declined. With this issue becoming more widespread, hopefully Apple and AT&T are working to inform employees about the issue and implement a formal process.

iPhone 18 Pro Max users should be aware that today is the final day to return the device to Apple under the company's standard 14-day return policy in the U.S., for customers who purchased or received it on September 18 launch day.

The Apple Watch Series 12 brings a more substantial set of changes than the Series 11, which was one of the smallest refreshes in the device's history. While Apple has discontinued previous Series models, older watches may still be available at lower prices from third-party retailers or secondhand.

Read on to see the breakdown below for each new feature, change, and improvement that was added with each Apple Watch model compared to its direct predecessor. The Series 12 has a stronger case than the Series 11 as an upgrade in general, but most Series 11 owners still have little reason to get a new device. Its new heart sensors, more frequent HRV measurements, Readiness app, and longer workout battery life matter most if you rely on your Apple Watch for training and recovery insights. Sound Recognition may also appeal to deaf or hard of hearing users, while the ceramic case offers a finish unavailable with the Series 11. 

Upgrading from a Series 10 brings these changes alongside the Series 11's 5G connectivity on cellular models and longer rated everyday battery life. From a Series 9, you would also gain the thinner Series 10 design, larger display, depth gauge, and water temperature sensor.

The cumulative upgrades become more compelling for Series 8 users and older, particularly if battery wear is affecting daily use. Series 7 owners gain Crash Detection and temperature sensing as well as the newer design and Series 12 health features. The biggest differences will be felt by those with a Series 6 or older, though the condition of your current watch and the cost of replacing it still matter.

watchOS 27 supports Series 9 and later, leaving the Series 8 and older without the latest major software release. That does not mean they will immediately stop working or receiving all security updates, but they are now considered old devices. If you are shopping for a replacement, a discounted or secondhand Series 11 may offer better value if you do not need the Series 12's health features, providing you can find it at a sufficiently low price. watchOS 26 is not supported by the Series 5 or older, so anyone with one of these devices should definitely consider upgrading soon.

title: AT&T floats a fix for iPhone cellular issues but it doesn’t appear to work
content:
Macworld





Following numerous complaints from iPhone 18 Pro Max owners, it’s now been officially acknowledged that some units have a problem placing calls, sending texts, and accessing data. Not by Apple itself, but by the carrier AT&T, which has sent out a message to customers warning about the issue and strongly advising them to update iOS “immediately”.
As seen by MacRumors, the carrier sent out the following text on Thursday:
“Hi, it’s AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately — Settings > General > Software Update. Please contact AT&T or Apple if you have questions.”
While this formal admission will be some comfort to affected parties–since the first step on the road to a fix is admitting that one is needed–the proposed solution may not be viewed kindly. Apple’s release notes for the iOS 27.0.1 software update do not mention fixing this issue, which is hardly a surprise given that the company (unlike AT&T) hasn’t yet acknowledged it. And many users who’ve encountered the bug explicitly report that updating to 27.0.1 doesn’t fix it.
The problem was first reported in mid-September. “New [iPhone 18 Pro Max] can’t make or receive phone calls or FaceTime,” complained the author of one Apple Support discussion thread. “Text messages are extremely slow to come through… It does all of this even when the phone is showing four bars of 5G… then the phone randomly drops service and goes into SOS.”
A Redditor, meanwhile, wrote: “I got my iPhone 18 on Friday. I have coverage through AT&T. I have been noticing that I have been getting SOS on my phone. Wi-Fi works for the internet but I can’t make calls. Even if it doesn’t say SOS, trying to make a phone call is impossible now.”
There are thousands of replies to these and similar discussions, many of whom confirm they’ve had the same experience. And they are pessimistic about AT&T’s solution. One commenter on the Apple Support thread replies, “I just received a text from them that the latest [iOS 27.0.1] update would fix the problem – I had already updated to this so I know it isn’t the resolution. This just reaffirms that they have no idea what the problem is or how to fix it.”
And while a separate Reddit thread entitled “iPhone 18 Pro Max Cellular Issues: Did iOS 27.0.1 resolve them?” includes a couple of replies who cautiously think it may have helped, but overwhelming people are unconvinced the issue is fixed:
“No, it did not fix that issue. Can confirm personally.”
“No… The bugfix update did nothing.”
“I feel like the 27.0.1 update made it worse.”
“I did the update but still have the problem.”
“I’m still having the issue even after the update, so it’s definitely AT&T.”
“I updated and it didn’t fix it and had to get the phone replaced for SECOND time.”
It would appear that we’re not even close to a resolution, since it isn’t even clear if this is a hardware or software problem, or whether it’s possible to fix it through an iOS update. We’ll keep you updated as we hear more.
Update, October 2: AT&T sent us the following statement:
“Apple has released a software update to address an issue that may affect calls, data, texts and 911 calls on a small number of Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max phones. AT&T customers with an iPhone 18 Pro Max should update their phones now to the latest available software. Our top priority is ensuring customers can stay connected when they need it most, and we are working with Apple to make it right.”

title: Apple is selling a $19 fix for iPhone Duo creasing
content:
Macworld





Apple has done as much as it can to minimize the visibility of the crease on the iPhone Duo, including multiple shifting display layers and a matte nano-texture surface that reduces glare and makes the crease less visible. But physics is what it is, and you just can’t fold and unfold a display thousands of times without any visible crease forming. The good news is, Apple has another solution to help mitigate that: a replaceable outer layer.
Speaking to @angietutorials on TikTok, Apple’s VP of hardware engineering, Kate Bergeron said, “the matte layer does a really nice job of, I’ll say minimizing the crease, but there’s a cover layer on top and we’ve done a significant amount of engineering work to help that wear in as long a manner as we can, to make sure you get the most out of that layer’s performance. It’s actually replaceable, which is a really nice thing for the customer, that you can peel off that layer and get a new one.”
The AppleCare service and repair site has already been updated with the costs of some repairs for the iPhone Duo with AppleCare+, and it looks like it’s only $19 to get the cover layer replaced. Just note, the top cover layer is not user replaceable like a screen protector would be, though, so don’t go peeling off your iPhone Duo display by yourself.
Apple does not yet list the cost of this service if you don’t have AppleCare+, but it is common for outer glass repairs or replacements to cost $100-150 more without coverage.

title: Best iPhone 18 cases for iPhone 18 Pro & 18 Pro Max
content:

You waited months for Apple’s new iPhones to arrive, but it’s worth protecting that big investment from day one. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are tougher than previous generations, but they can still be scratched, chipped or damaged in a drop. A good case also does more than protect your phone: it can improve grip, add a stand or wallet, support MagSafe accessories and give your iPhone a completely different look.
There are thousands of iPhone cases to choose from, ranging from inexpensive silicone shells to rugged cases built for serious drop protection. Price isn’t always a reliable guide to quality, either: a cheap case can split, yellow or develop faulty buttons, while spending more doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the best case for your needs.
That’s why we hand-test and compare as many iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max cases as we can. We consider protection, materials, build quality, grip, raised screen and camera edges, MagSafe compatibility, weight, useful extras such as stands and card storage, and how the case feels in everyday use. Where manufacturers make specific drop-protection claims, we include those too so you can compare different levels of protection.
In this guide we’ve grouped our recommendations into clear, colorful, protective and leather or faux-leather cases, with options at a range of prices.

Which type of iPhone case to choose
Apple gives you a handful of finishes; a case gives you thousands—an easy way to make an iPhone 18 Pro look like yours. You can choose a clear case that shows off the iPhone’s original color but adds vital protection, or choose a case with more personality. Protection is key, and some cases will add higher levels of defense than others.
Beyond looks, think about how you use your phone. Want hands-free video? Look for a case with a built-in stand. Want to leave your wallet at home? Choose one with a card storage wallet. And if you charge wirelessly, check for MagSafe compatibility — most cases now offer it, and it’s worth confirming before you buy.


						

							




Best clear cases for iPhone 18

Zagg has a whole range of popular scratch-resistant clear case models for the iPhone 18 Pro series, including the Crystal Palace Snap, available with and without a kickstand) and a simpler Lite option without MagSafe and lower but still impressive drop protection. Zagg’s ClearGuard tech reduces the yellowing that affects many clear cases surprisingly quickly.
The Crystal Palace Snap ($54.99 / £39.99 with kickstand, $49.99 / £34.99 without) has textured sides for better grip, MagSafe, and 13ft drop protection. The Crystal Palace Lite Snap ($39.99 / £24.99) has MagSafe, 10ft drop protection and no kickstand. The entry-level Crystal Palace Lite ($29.99/ £19.99) lacks MagSafe and kickstand but still offers 10ft drop protection.
Both use PC and TPU, but the construction is fundamentally different. The premium Crystal Palace Snap uses a single, solid piece of PC across the back and sides to create a harder, more scratch-resistant clear case, with TPU used strategically so that there are no seams between the back and sides. Best protective cases for iPhone 18
As pretty as some iPhone cases are, your principal consideration should be protection. Most decent cases offer reasonable protection, but these protective cases have extra robust features while often adding as little bulk as possible by using the latest, strongest materials. Kevlar is the material used to make bulletproof vests—it’s also known as Aramid Fiber—but I wouldn’t try turning a rifle on it. Graphene is even stronger, and would probably make Superman wince trying to snap it in half.
Other protective iPhone cases don’t worry so much about thinness, and bulk up to protect your iPhone from the worst disasters that can befall it. These might suit you if you work in riskier environments or are an active outdoors iPhone user.
Material matters too: Graphene (elastic yet harder than diamond and up to 200x stronger than steel, according to case makers) or Kevlar (the material used to make bulletproof vests) for serious durability. Kevlar is a type of Aramid Fiber, a strong, heat-resistant synthetic material that gives the material incredible strength and stability.

 FAQ 


1.
What is Apple’s Ceramic Shield protection for iPhones?
Apple introduced Ceramic Shield with the iPhone 12 in 2020, developed jointly with glassmaker Corning, and it’s been standard on every iPhone since (excluding the budget SE line).
It’s made by fusing nano-ceramic crystals into glass, then dipping it in molten salt so potassium ions swap places with smaller sodium ions, creating a compressive surface layer that resists cracking. This gave the original iPhone 12 four times better drop performance than the iPhone 11.
Ceramic Shield 2 arrived with the iPhone 17 lineup in 2025, keeping the same crystal-infusion and ion-exchange process but with a refined composition that’s roughly three times more scratch-resistant than the first generation, while retaining similar drop protection. On the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Ceramic Shield 2 protects the front, while the back uses Ceramic Shield.





2.
Why do you need an iPhone case?
Your iPhone is a precision device that lives in an unpredictable world—pockets, bags, countertops, pavement. A case is what stands between an accidental drop and a cracked screen or shattered back. It’s not a small risk either: plenty of new iPhone owners crack a screen within the first ten weeks of ownership (source). The IP68 rating means real dust and water resistance, but that’s a lab result—real life is messier. Add in the daily wear of being pulled in and out of a pocket, plus UV exposure over time, and the damage adds up quietly. A case won’t make your iPhone indestructible, but it absorbs the everyday hits so you don’t end up paying for a repair — or a replacement.





3.
Will the iPhone 18 Pro fit a case for the iPhone 17 Pro?
The iPhone 18 Pro series are virtually identical to the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. Even my iPhone 16 Pro fits in an 18 Pro case, and it works just fine—it looks a bit weird at the back, but otherwise fits nicely. On the other hand, a 17 Pro or 18 Pro wouldn’t fit in a 16 Pro case because of the rear camera positioning. Rokform told Macworld that its iPhone 18 Pro case lineup is compatible with iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro models. However, its older iPhone 17 Pro case lineup is not compatible with iPhone 18 models due to camera plateau design differences. Cases designed with tight tolerances might therefore have a problem as the camera plateau on iPhone 18 Pro/Max is about 0.5mm taller than on iPhone 17 Pro/Max.
Leading case manufacturer OtterBox reports that its iPhone 18 Pro/Max cases are “also compatible with iPhone 17 Pro, so the cases can be used interchangeably between those two models”.
New cases are custom-built for each device to guarantee a perfect fit and protection, so buying a case built specifically for your iPhone model is the safest option. Check our roundup of the Best iPhone 17 Cases and Best iPhone 16 Cases for the older models.





4.
Do I need a screen protector if I use a case?
Yes, it’s still worth using a screen protector even if you have a case, as the two provide different but complementary protection. A case protects the back, corners, and edges of your iPhone, while a screen protector is designed to protect the display itself from scratches and cracks. 
Tempered-glass screen protectors can help absorb direct impacts and protect against everyday scratches and abrasions. A case with a raised screen lip offers some protection if your iPhone lands face down, but it can’t prevent every object or surface from making direct contact with the screen.





5.
What type of iPhone case offers the best protection?
When it comes to maximum protection for your iPhone, the clear winners are rugged cases built with multi-layer materials and military-grade drop ratings. Rugged cases typically combine a hard polycarbonate outer shell with a shock-absorbing TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) inner layer, reinforced corners, and raised edges around both the screen and camera to prevent direct surface contact on drops.
While silicone and leather cases offer decent everyday scratch protection, they simply can’t match the impact resistance of a purpose-built rugged case.
When choosing a protective case, look for:
Raised screen edge around the front (at least 1mm) to keep the screen safely off surfaces.
Raised camera edge (0.5mm minimum, some go up to 3.6mm).
MIL-STD-810G certification — a U.S. Department of Defense standard for durability.
Reinforced corners for impact absorption.
MagSafe compatibility if you wirelessly charge.





6.
Do I need an iPhone case for iPhone 18?
Many consumers damage their devices each year, with cracked, chipped or shattered screens the leading reason for iPhone repairs. A screen protector is an important first line of defense, but a case with a raised screen edge can much better protect the display from everyday knocks and drops, and tough sides and back will reduce the risk of damage from an accidental fall.
Ceramic Shield 2, introduced with the iPhone 17 generation, protects the front of the iPhone 18 Pro and offers three times better scratch resistance than the iPhone 16 Pro. The back uses Ceramic Shield, which Apple says offers four times better crack resistance than the back glass used on earlier models.
The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are the best-protected iPhones yet, but a case is still worth buying. It helps keep that pristine finish looking new and, when it’s time to trade up, a well-protected iPhone can retain far more resale value than the cost of the case itself.





How we test iPhone cases
When we receive new cases, we test them for fit, button feel, grip, MagSafe strength and alignment, raised-edge camera and screen protection, bulk, weight, and day-to-day handling. Where we are unable to test a case ourselves, we assess it based on its specifications and our experience with other cases from the same manufacturer that have impressed us. We report manufacturers’ claimed drop-protection metrics. As we have listed iPhone cases only from trusted companies we feel safe in these claims but note that measurement is the maker’s own and not ours or Apple’s.

title: Apple’s September was huge. October could be even bigger
content:
Macworld





The big September Apple event is over and the new iPhones have been announced, which usually means a little quiet. Not this year. While the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shipped last month, the star of the show, the iPhone Duo, hasn’t even gone up for pre-order yet.
But that’s not all—there’s a good chance we’re going to see some other new hardware, too. Plus, we’ve got the OS 27.2 updates in testing now with a big update to the Health app, and those will probably be released in October as well. Plus the Matchbox movie premieres! Here’s everything that’s coming in October:
iPhone Duo and other new hardware
We already know Apple has one monster release coming this month, but several other new products could be on the way as well:
iPhone Duo: Pre-orders for Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, begin on October 16 and the phone officially becomes available on October 23. Obviously that is going to be the big release of the month, and you can read a lot more about the iPhone Duo in our guide. If you want one, you’ll want to pre-order right when it goes on sale at 8am ET, because we expect stock will be very constrained throughout the rest of this year.
Smart home hub: Leading this month’s rumors is a totally new device we’ve been hearing about for years: a home hub many have taken to calling “HomePad.” It’s a simplified tablet with a roughly 6-inch display that runs a new operating system combining the Standby mode of iPhone, the widgets of Apple Watch, and some of the media capabilities of Apple TV, but without its own app store. It will reportedly control your smart home devices, make FaceTime calls, and recognize faces to automatically adjust to each individual’s preferences. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the most reliable Apple leaker around, says the device is set to launch on October 13.
HomePod mini 2: Along with the hub, there are persistent rumors of other smart home devices ready to go on sale in October, including a new HomePod mini. The HomePod mini 2 should have a new processor that supports Siri AI, improved networking, and improved audio, but visually resemble the current model, which hasn’t been updated since its 2020 debut. It will likely have a new lineup of colors.
Apple TV 4K (4th gen): The new Apple TV 4K is getting the same treatment: better networking and a faster chip for Siri AI, but otherwise the same as the current models. Some say that the remote might support Find My, with a tiny speaker to make a chime when lost.
iPad mini: Several rumors also claim the next iPad mini is nearly ready for release, with an A20 Pro, OLED display, and landscape-oriented FaceTime camera. It would be a big upgrade, and the most recent rumors say it will launch by the end of October.
M6 MacBook Pro: The M6 has debuted in the Mac mini, and it has been a year since the M5 MacBook Pro, so we now expect a MacBook Pro with M6 to come as early as October. It should be a chip update with the same design.
Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Separate from the regular M6 MacBook Pro, there’s a redesigned MacBook Pro allegedly in the works with an OLED display and a touchscreen. Multiple reports have said it could be ready for release this fall with M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, but chip shortages could also push it into next year.
Apps and software updates
We just got Apple’s biggest yearly software update in ages with last month’s OS 27 launches with the new Siri AI, but there’s a big change coming to it soon.
While the iOS 27.1 release is centered around iPhone Duo and will likely only ship with that device, the OS 27.2 updates — coming for all devices — is already in beta testing and should be widely released in the month of October. The big update for 27.2 is the overhauled Health app, which changes the design to put AI-powered health analysis up front, with collected data on a later tab. With an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4 and watchOS 27.2, you’ll also get the new Readiness feature.
Services
Apple TV+
Here are the shows, series, and movies we expect to release on Apple TV+ in TK. If you want to know what’s coming later, check our full guide to upcoming Apple TV+ content.
The Last First: Winter K2: A documentary about the extreme mountain climbing industry and its changing culture. October 2
The Sisters Grimm (season 2): Two orphaned sisters navigate a town full of people torn straight from fantasy and fairy tales, confronting heroes and villains alike, while investigating the mystery of their missing parents. October 2
Small Prophets: Michael Sleep is still struggling after his girlfriend, Clea, vanished seven years earlier. Sleep works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian, and hopes for Clea’s return. October 7
Matchbox the Movie: Inspired by the iconic Mattel toys (really!), this is an action film about a group of friends since childhood who have their lives upended when undercover CIA agent Sean, their long-absent former leader, returns to their small town and unwittingly gets them embroiled in a frantic international pursuit to save the world. October 9
Tenzing: Chronicles the little-known story of Tenzing Norgay, a gifted Himalayan climber who, alongside New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary, became the first to summit Mount Everest. October 16
Where’s Wanda (season 2): A dark comedy that tells the story of Dedo and Carlotta Klatt, who are desperate to locate their missing 17-year-old daughter Wanda, who disappeared months ago without a trace. October 21
Nocturne: The series tells the story of an ex-soldier turned homicide detective Jonah Lynn who moves to a small town in western Pennsylvania for a quiet life. But as the town and his family come under attack from the diabolically cunning serial killer Jurek Walter, Jonah must protect all that he holds dear. October 30
Apple Arcade
Apple releases most Apple Arcade games on the first Friday of each month. Check our Apple Arcade FAQ for a full list of Apple Arcade games and more details on the service. Occasionally, games are released with no forewarning, but you’ll usually see next month’s releases listed in the Coming Soon section.
4 Pics 1 Word+: Puzzle game where you guess the one word associated with 4 images. October 1
Pusheen’s Place: Collect cute cats and decorate their home in this cozy game. October 1
River City Survivors: A Vampire Survivors-like game using the River City game setting. October 1
Terraria+: The popular and massive dig-and-build game comes to Apple Arcade. October 1
Touchgrind BMX 2+: Race and do tricks with those little finger-sized dirtbikes. October 1

title: ‘Halo’ and the missed opportunity for the Mac
content:
Macworld





Halo, officially known as Halo: Combat Evolved, was released for the Xbox in 2001. It’s regarded as the game that perfected the first-person shooter on the console, after GoldenEye 007 for the Nintendo 64 had provided the first successful blueprint four years earlier. Yet things could have turned out very differently.
Originally, Halo was unveiled for the Mac at Macworld Expo in July 1999. Alongside other titles, Halo was set to become a flagship for gaming on the Mac. This was no coincidence: the developer, Bungie had made a name for itself on the Mac in previous years with Marathon and Myth. Gaming on the Mac wasn’t exactly a novelty back then. And so Jason Jones, co-founder of Bungie, presented the first gameplay footage of Halo, complete with Martin O’Donnell’s now-iconic theme tune, on a Mac, specifically, the Power Macintosh G3.
Jones was introduced by Steve Jobs himself, who also announced that Halo would be released “early next year,” (early 2000). But things turned out differently.


27 years on, the first gameplay footage from ‘Halo: Combat Evolved’ seems almost prehistoric.



Microsoft buys Bungie
At the same time, Microsoft was planning something quite different. In PC gaming, Apple’s direct competitor had long since established itself and was setting its sights on game consoles. Microsoft wanted to shake up that market, which at the time was dominated by Nintendo, Sony (PlayStation) and, to a lesser extent, Sega (Dreamcast). To succeed, the company had to win gamers over to its platform and offer an attractive game library featuring top-class titles at the console’s launch.
The unveiling of Halo at Macworld Expo came at just the right time. On the one hand, the title promised to breathe new life into the first-person shooter genre; on the other, it was backed by a team that, whilst not as large or well-known as id Software (Doom, Quake), nevertheless already had a solid portfolio to its name. So Microsoft bought Bungie, along with Halo, and the game was not released for the Mac and only for the Xbox in late 2001.
Halo: Combat Evolved did eventually come out for the Mac in 2003, but no further Halo installment has since made it onto an Apple platform natively, even though the series was originally intended for it. You can only play all the titles on Apple devices via the cloud, but to do so you’ll need either Xbox Game Pass Ultimate for Xbox Cloud Gaming or GeForce Now. At least that means you can even play Halo on your iPhone.
The best for (almost) everyone
Halo could have given Mac gaming the boost it needed, but Apple’s gaming dilemma is of its own making. One game wouldn’t have made any difference. It would also be presumptuous to believe that Halo alone could have elevated the platform to a relevant level. After all, many other games–some of which were already better known at the time–were announced back in 1999.
Looking back, Microsoft’s acquisition of Bungie was a great success. Microsoft managed to break into the console market and took Sega’s place, whose Dreamcast flop in 2001 also sealed the company’s fate as a hardware manufacturer.
Halo, on the other hand, established itself as the flagship title for first-person shooters on consoles and brought Bungie immense fame and success within the games industry. Following its split from Microsoft in 2007 and a partnership with Activision since 2010, the studio has, as of 2022, been owned by none other than Sony, Microsoft’s biggest rival in the console market.
And Apple? The company hasn’t completely abandoned its gaming ambitions, but the whole endeavor has been languishing for years. Although Apple makes a decent profit in the sector, it does not operate like a traditional gaming company and almost exclusively as a marketing platform, earning its revenue primarily through commissions from the App Store and in-app purchases. The subscription fees for Apple Arcade won’t feature prominently in the balance sheet.
Still, even without Halo, Apple is posting new record profits year after year. On the whole, things have gone quite well for all three parties involved.

title: Lamtto RC37 CarPlay Auto Display review: For old cars
content:
Macworld





At a glance

Our Verdict 
Anyone looking to retrofit an older vehicle with CarPlay and who has sufficient space in the cockpit will find the Lamtto Car Infotainment System to be a solution featuring a large screen, flexible audio output and, as a bonus, a back camera.
